problem: Classical modular stacks such as ROS Nav2 need heavy per-deployment tuning and fail in cluttered or narrow settings, where they show indecision between homotopy classes. End-to-end imitation-learning navigators suffer covariate shift and generalize poorly out of distribution. World-model methods from driving (e.g. MILE) are limited by the scarcity of large expert-labelled robot navigation datasets.
motivation: A navigation stack should work across environments and robot bodies and run on edge compute. The authors observe two things: world models learn dynamics that help robustness under distribution shift, and dynamics can be learned from cheap off-policy (random-action) data. So separating world modeling from policy imitation lets large unlabeled data shape the latent state, while scarce expert data only has to train the policy head.
key_idea: Train a lightweight RSSM-style probabilistic latent world model on a DINOv2 encoder. It is first trained on random-action synthetic data, with semantic-segmentation and RGB-diffusion decoders shaping the latent. An imitation policy that fuses the latent state with a VectorNet-encoded route is then trained on Nav2 teacher data to output continuous velocity commands.
insight: Most of the out-of-distribution robustness comes from how the latent state is trained, not from the policy head. Ablations on the random-obstacle (OOD) scenes show this. Removing world-model pretraining on 160K random-action frames drops SR 68→44. Removing the semantic decoder drops SR 68→36, even though it slightly improves in-distribution warehouse results (SR 96, WTT 33.7 vs 37.7), which suggests overfitting. Resetting the recurrent history each cycle drops SR to 72 (warehouse) and 16 (random obstacles). Open-loop MAE is nearly identical across MILE, BC and X-Mobility (MILE even has the best L-MAE) while closed-loop SR differs greatly (34 vs 92 vs 96), so open-loop imitation error is a poor proxy for navigation quality.
method: Observation encoding: a DINOv2 image encoder (22.1M params, fine-tuned) turns front RGB into a 768-d token (class token concatenated with average-pooled patch tokens). An FC layer encodes linear speed to 32-d, giving o_t=[u_t, m_t].

State estimation network (RSSM-like): a GRU history h_t (1024-d) plus MLP Normal-distribution heads give a 512-d stochastic belief s_t ~ N(μ(h_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_t), σ); the action is embedded via MLP (64-d). The latent is z_t=[h_{t-1}, s_t]. It runs fully recurrently at deployment and is trained on 5-frame auto-regressive sequences.

State prediction network: the same GRU + Normal structure without observation input, trained with a KL loss (weight 0.001, balancing α 0.75) to match the estimator's belief. This enables multi-step latent rollouts, decodable to semantics.

Multi-task decoders: a StyleGAN-style progressive upsampler from a learned constant decodes 7-class perspective-view semantic segmentation (CE loss at every resolution). A fine-tuned latent diffusion model (962M params) conditioned on z_t reconstructs RGB (noise MSE loss).

Route encoding: the global route (straight line or topological-graph waypoints) is transformed into the robot frame and truncated to a local 20×2 segment. VectorNet (4 layers) encodes it to a 64-d embedding, avoiding a map and a costly route search.

Action policy: self-attention fuses z_t with the route embedding into a 2048-d policy state. MLPs decode a 6-d velocity command (linear + angular x,y,z) and an optional 5-pose path, trained with L1 imitation of the Nav2 teacher (weights 10 and 5). A diffusion-policy head variant was also tried.

Multi-stage training: stage 1 trains the world model for 100 epochs on 160K random-action frames using logged actions, with the policy disabled. Stage 2 jointly trains the policy and world model for 100 epochs on 100K Nav2 teacher frames with the RGB diffuser disabled. Training uses 8×H100, batch 32, AdamW lr 1e-5, OneCycleLR.

setting.backbone: DINOv2 image encoder (fine-tuned) + GRU/RSSM-style latent world model + self-attention/MLP action policy, trained with imitation learning
setting.model_size: Per-module parameter counts: image encoder 22.1M, state estimator 5.5M, state predictor 2.3M, self-attention fuser 28.5M, action decoder 10.5M, path decoder 10.5M, semantic decoder 34.2M, RGB diffuser 962M (disabled during policy training)
setting.training_data: Synthetic Isaac Sim data from a Nova Carter robot in 4 warehouse environments with randomized textures, layouts and lighting, recorded at 5Hz: 160K frames of random-action (off-policy) data plus 100K frames from a closed-loop ROS Nav2 teacher with random start/goal pairs. Each frame carries RGB 320×512, speed, 7-class semantic labels, route, path and action command.
setting.observation: monocular front-view RGB + robot linear speed + local route waypoints in the robot frame (requires localization)
setting.action_space: continuous velocity commands (6-d linear/angular velocity) plus an optional 5-pose local path; executed by a diff-drive controller or pre-trained RL locomotion policies on other embodiments
setting.privileged: No map or ground-truth semantics at test time. It does need robot localization and a given global route (straight line to goal or topological waypoints); in simulation, pose/route presumably come from the simulator.

numbers_note: All results are on the authors' own Isaac Sim warehouse benchmark; no standard embodied-navigation benchmark is used. Metrics: SR (%), WTT = weighted trip time (s, trip time / SR), AA = mean absolute angular acceleration (rad/s²). The 'X-Mobility w/ DP' variant (diffusion policy head) is reported only open-loop (Table I: A-MAE 0.0306, L-MAE 0.1115, P-MAE 0.0389); closed-loop it is described only qualitatively as failing. Real-robot results (Table 'Benchmark on real robot', Nova Carter, zero-shot) are given as counts, not percentages: Single Obstacle/Normal 10/10 (AA 0.267), Single Obstacle/Dark 10/10 (AA 0.267), Multi Obstacles/Normal 8/9 (AA 0.205), Multi Obstacles/Dark 8/9 (AA 0.273). Jetson AGX Orin latency: Policy Only P50 38.6 ms / P95 41.96 ms / 594 MB; Policy + Semantic P50 55.55 ms / P95 55.72 ms / 804 MB. Semantic IoU is in Table III. Multi-step prediction IoU and the cross-embodiment results (Carter, forklift, Go2, G1) appear only in figures or qualitatively.
results: In closed loop, X-Mobility reaches 96% SR (WTT 37.7 s, AA 0.206) in warehouse scenarios and 68% SR (WTT 40.21 s) in the 50 OOD random-obstacle scenes. The strongest baseline, a BC model with the same DINOv2 encoder, gets 92% and 56%. The Nav2 teacher gets 58% and 34%, and a perspective-view MILE adaptation gets 34% and 26%. The model transfers zero-shot to a real Nova Carter (10/10 single-obstacle, 8/9 multi-obstacle, in normal and dark lighting), runs at about 39 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin, and is shown qualitatively driving quadruped, humanoid and Ackermann platforms in simulation.
limitations: Evaluated only on a custom benchmark in warehouse-style scenes with static obstacles (4 training environments, 50 runs per setting); no comparison on standard embodied-navigation benchmarks, and dynamic obstacles are left to future work.

Requires robot localization and a given global route; it is a local route-following/obstacle-avoidance policy, not goal search or semantic navigation. Cross-embodiment results are only qualitative, and performance depends on camera placement.

The diffusion-policy head degraded linear commands and was unstable in closed loop; removing the semantic decoder improves in-distribution results, which hints that the policy can overfit the training warehouses.
